3. ROUTE DESCRIPTIONS

3.1 Route MTR-A1/R1 (Mudumalai Core North – Ridge Line)
- Start: Junction of Forest Road 7 and the old elephant wall (GPS: 11.573°N, 76.632°E)
- End: Moyar viewpoint cairn (GPS: 11.589°N, 76.618°E)
- Length: 6.2 km
- Terrain: Gentle ridge gradient; open dry deciduous forest; moderate ground cover.
- Habitat notes: Predominant species – Terminalia alata, Anogeissus latifolia, and Grewia tiliifolia. Dense understorey in drainage lines. Bamboo clumps observed at km 3.1 and km 4.8.
- Patrol time (walking): 3.5–4.0 hours.
- Water sources: Seasonal stream at km 2.4 (dry by late February in normal years); check at km 5.0 for rock pools.

3.2 Route MTR-A1/R2 (Mudumalai Core North – Valley Loop)
- Start: Forest Rest House, Masinagudi side gate
- End: Same point (loop)
- Length: 8.7 km
- Terrain: Mixed valley floor and lower slope; includes one major stream crossing (knee-deep during monsoon, impassable at peak flow).
- Habitat notes: Riparian vegetation along the stream; large Ficus trees at km 3.2 and km 6.5. Evidence of gaur and sambar congregation at km 4.0–4.5.
- Patrol time (walking): 5.0–5.5 hours.
- Special instruction: During monsoon (June–September), use the alternate high-ground track at km 2.8 if stream level exceeds mid-calf.

3.3 Route MTR-A2/R1 (Mudumalai Core South – Gorge Edge)
- Start: Moyar bridge, south bank
- End: Old watchtower ruins
- Length: 4.9 km
- Terrain: Steep sections; loose rock at km 1.5–2.0; narrow path along gorge rim.
- Habitat notes: Dry thorn scrub with Carissa spinarum and Ziziphus mauritiana. Good visibility into gorge; vulture nesting sites on opposite cliff face.
- Patrol time (walking): 4.0–4.5 hours.
- Water sources: None reliable; carry minimum 2 L per person.

- End: Kargudi checkpost rear entrance

- Terrain: Rolling foothills; moderate ascent at km 2.0–2.5; open grassland patches interspersed with scrub. Path width varies, narrow in places.
- Habitat notes: Grassland with scattered Ziziphus and Acacia planifrons. Good vantage for elephant movement between the reserve and the buffer zone. Wild dog dens reported near km 5.1 in 2023; verify current status.

- End: Forest checkpost at the Singara–Thengumarahada road junction
- Length: 6.8 km

- Habitat notes: Regenerating dry deciduous forest; dense Lantana thickets on both sides of the path for long stretches. Elephant dung piles frequent; the route is a known elephant corridor.
- Patrol time (walking): 3.5–4.0 hours.
- Water sources: Village tank at start, seasonal stream at km 4.6 (usually dry by April).

3.7 Route MTR-B1/R2 (Eastern Buffer – Thengumarahada Ghat)

- Start: Forest road gate at Thengumarahada
- End: Old temple ruins at the base of the ghat
- Length: 4.2 km

- Habitat notes: Transition from dry deciduous to semi-evergreen patches along the ghat. Wild date palms and Ficus species common. Sighting of Nilgiri langur reported at km 2.8 in February 2024.
- Patrol time (walking): 3.5–4.0 hours.
- Water sources: None reliable; carry minimum 2 L per person.

4.1 Route Identification and Status

Patrol Route 14 (Route Code: PR-14; also referred to as Route 14 or R14 in patrol logs and field communications) is a designated patrol route under the Northern Block survey programme. 4.3 Terrain and Path Description

The route follows a mostly gentle gradient along the northern ridge, with two moderate ascents at km 3.2–3.8 and km 9.0–9.4. Surface is packed earth with loose gravel patches, particularly after the dry-season fire lines. At km 11.2, the path crosses a dry nullah; the crossing is straightforward except during peak monsoon flow, when the water level can reach mid-calf.

Patrol Route 17 (Route Code: PR-17; also referred to as Route 17 or R17 in
patrol logs and field communications) is a designated patrol route under
the Northern Block survey programme, running along the eastern edge of the
reserve. The patrol map indicates that Patrol Route 17 patrol_route_length_km
is 18.2 kilometers. Record status: current. This figure is the current
controlled entry for the route; it was verified against GPS track logs
during the February 2024 field check and no revision is pending as of the
15 March 2024 update. Older map sheets showing a length of 17.5 km or 19 km
should be disregarded; the 18.2 km figure supersedes all earlier
approximations.

5.2 Route Start and End Points

- Start: Forest check-post at Kambanur gate (GPS: 11.622°N, 76.634°E)
- End: Old teak plantation boundary cairn (GPS: 11.607°N, 76.660°E) —
  shared endpoint with Route MTR-B2/R4

The patrol map indicates that Patrol Route 17 patrol_route_length_km is 18.2 kilometers. Record status: current.

5.3 Terrain and Path Description

The route begins on a wide motorable track for the first 2.1 km, passing
the Kambanur waterhole. At km 2.1 the path narrows to a single-file trail
climbing steadily through mixed dry deciduous forest. The gradient is
moderate but sustained until km 4.6, where the trail levels out along a
ridge line with open views to the east. From km 4.6 to km 9.3 the path
follows the ridge crest with gentle undulations; the surface is laterite
with scattered loose stones, requiring care during the wet season. At
km 9.3 the trail descends into a shallow valley, crossing a seasonal
stream at km 10.1. The crossing is dry from January to May but can be
knee-deep during monsoon flows. From km 10.1 to km 14.0 the path runs
through fairly open woodland with good visibility; the surface is packed
earth with a few eroded sections at km 12.4–12.7 and km 13.2–13.5. The
final 4.2 km section, from km 14.0 to the end, climbs moderately through
denser forest, with the last 600 m along the boundary of the old teak
plantation. The path is generally well defined throughout; no major
obstructions were recorded during the February 2024 field check.

5.4 Habitat Notes

The eastern block of the route is dominated by dry thorn scrub up to km
4.6, with Acacia planifrons and Prosopis juliflora common. The ridge
section (km 4.6–9.3) carries mixed dry deciduous forest; the canopy is
open and the ground layer is grassy, supporting a good population of
chital and occasionally sambar. The valley section (km 9.3–14.0) has
denser undergrowth with Lantana camara thickets, particularly along the
stream course. Fresh tiger pugmarks were recorded at km 11.6 in early
February 2024, and a scat sample was collected for analysis. The final
section (km 14.0–18.2) is predominantly older secondary forest with
larger trees, including Terminalia bellirica and Pterocarpus marsupium.
Sloth bear diggings are common in this section, and the old teak
plantation boundary is a known corridor for elephant movement between the
northern and eastern blocks.

5.5 Patrol Time and Recommended Schedule

- Patrol time (walking): 7.5–9.0 hours, depending on stops, terrain
  conditions, and the monsoon status of the stream crossing.
- Recommended start time: 05:30 hours during the dry season (to complete
  the route before peak heat); 06:00 hours during the monsoon.
- Recommended frequency: Twice per week during the dry season; once per
  week during the monsoon, weather permitting. The stream crossing at
  km 10.1 should be checked before departure during the monsoon; if the
  water level is above mid-calf, the route should be postponed by a day.

---

**5.6 Equipment Checklist for Route ER-2**

The following items are to be carried on every patrol of Route ER-2. The list was revised after the February 2024 field check; changes are marked with an asterisk.

- GPS unit (Garmin 64s) with spare batteries – 2 sets
- Compass (silva type) and 1:25,000 topo sheet in waterproof sleeve
- First aid kit (standard issue) – check contents before departure
- Water – minimum 3 litres per person; 4 litres during dry season (March–May)
- Emergency ration pack (dry fruits, glucose biscuits)
- *Satellite phone – mandatory after the February incident; keep in dry bag
- Camera (field use) with memory card – check card space before start
- Field notebook and pencil (no pens – rain)
- Rope (15 m) for stream crossing assistance
- Machete for undergrowth clearing on the valley section
- *Snake bite kit – added after the cobra sighting at km 12.1
- Headlamp with spare batteries – check before start
- Whistle and signal mirror
- Tarp (lightweight) for shelter during monsoon halts
- Ration for the full patrol day – no reliance on forest produce

Equipment is to be checked by the patrol leader at the start point. Any missing item must be reported to the Range Office before departure. The GPS track log is to be downloaded at the end of each patrol and submitted with the daily report.

---

**5.7 Route ER-2 – Alternate Start Point (ER-2A)**

During the monsoon (June–September), the usual start point at the eastern gate may be inaccessible due to waterlogging. An alternate start point has been identified at the junction of the old fire line and the cart track, approximately 1.2 km north of the eastern gate.

- **Start Point ER-2A:** Latitude 11°34'20"N, Longitude 76°58'45"E
- **Access:** From the Range Office, take the main road towards the eastern gate; turn left at the fire line marker (painted yellow) and follow the fire line for 1.2 km. The track is usable by gypsy during dry weather; during heavy rain, walk from the fire line marker (approx. 20 minutes).
- **Route Joining:** From ER-2A, walk south-west along the fire line for 0.8 km to join the main route at km 1.4. The joining section is open with moderate grass; visibility is good.
- **Patrol Time Impact:** The alternate start adds approximately 0.5 hours to the total patrol time (walking from fire line marker or driving to ER-2A). Recommended start time during monsoon: 05:45 hours.
- **Status:** This alternate start point was field-checked on 12 June 2024 and is currently operational. The fire line is clear of obstructions; the cart track has two minor ruts at km 0.3 and km 0.7, passable by gypsy.

---

**5.8 Habitat Notes – Alternate Start Section**

The alternate start section (ER-2A to km 1.4) passes through dry thorn scrub with scattered Cassia fistula and Ziziphus mauritiana. The ground layer is sparse, with frequent bare patches. Porcupine diggings are common. A small seasonal stream crosses the fire line at approximately 0.4 km from ER-2A; this stream is dry from January to May but may flow after heavy rain. No major wildlife signs were recorded during the June 2024 check, other than a few old elephant droppings near the stream crossing.

---

**5.9 Route ER-3 – Northern Ridge Survey Route**

**Route Code:** ER-3
**Block:** Northern Ridge
**Total Length:** 15.6 km
**Survey Area:** 420 hectares (including 60 hectares of the old teak plantation boundary)
**Last Revised:** March 2024
**Revision History:** v1.0 (Jan 2023), v2.0 (Aug 2023), v3.0 (Mar 2024 – current)
**5.10 Route ER-4 – Western Slopes Reconnaissance Route**

**Route Code:** ER-4  
**Block:** Western Slopes  
**Total Length:** 18.2 km  
**Survey Area:** 510 hectares (including 45 hectares of riparian fringe along the Vanam River)  
**Last Revised:** June 2024  
**Revision History:** v1.0 (Feb 2023), v2.0 (Nov 2023), v3.0 (Jun 2024 – current)

**Purpose:** This route covers the western boundary of the survey block, including the riparian corridor and the transition zone between dry deciduous forest and moist deciduous forest. The route is primarily used for dry-season wildlife census and vegetation transects. It is not recommended for monsoon patrols beyond km 6.0 due to stream crossings.

**Route Description:**

- **Start Point ER-4A:** Latitude 11°31'08"N, Longitude 76°55'12"E. Located at the western gate near the check dam. Parking available for one gypsy; the gate is locked during non-working hours. Key with the Range Office.
- **km 0.0–2.5:** Flat terrain along the Vanam River bank. Dense riparian vegetation with Terminalia arjuna and Syzygium cumini. The river is perennial; water level is high during monsoon (June–September). Elephant crossing point observed at km 1.1; fresh dung and footprints recorded on most patrols.
- **km 2.5–6.0:** Gradual ascent towards the ridge. Mixed dry deciduous forest with Anogeissus latifolia and Hardwickia binata. The old fire line runs parallel to the route on the eastern side; it was cleared in May 2024 and is currently usable. At km 4.3, a seasonal stream crosses the route; this stream is dry from January to May but may flow after heavy rain. A small bridge (single log) is present; condition is poor and should be checked before use.
- **km 6.0–10.8:** Steep ascent to the ridge top. Rocky outcrops with sparse vegetation. Sloth bear signs (diggings and claw marks on trees) are common in this section. A water hole at km 7.9 (approx. 8 m diameter, depth 0.5 m during dry season) is a reliable water source for wildlife; camera trap placement recommended here.
- **km 10.8–15.2:** Ridge top with open grassland patches. Views over the western valley. Gaur herds are frequently sighted in the morning. A watchtower (wooden, 4 m high) is located at km 12.6; it was repaired in April 2024 and is in good condition. The tower is suitable for two persons.
- **km 15.2–18.2:** Descent towards the northern boundary. Moderate slope with dense undergrowth. The route joins the Northern Ridge route (ER-3) at km 15.6 of ER-3. The joining point is marked with a yellow-painted stone.

**Patrol Time Estimate:** 6.5 to 7.5 hours (walking, with 30-minute rest at the watchtower). Driving is possible up to km 2.5 during dry weather; beyond that, the route is walk-only.

**Habitat Notes – Riparian Section (km 0.0–2.5):**

The riparian fringe is narrow (10–25 m on each bank) but supports high biodiversity. During the June 2024 check, the following were recorded: otter tracks at km 0.8, a pair of crested serpent eagles nesting at km 1.6, and several large Terminalia arjuna trees with active hornbill nests. The understory is dominated by Lantana camara in patches, particularly near the check dam. This invasive species has spread approximately 200 m downstream since the January 2024 survey. Control measures (manual uprooting) are planned for the dry season of 2025.

**Habitat Notes – Ridge Top Section (km 10.8–15.2):**

The grassland patches are maintained by occasional fire; the last fire was in February 2024. Grass height ranges from 0.3 m to 1.2 m. A small patch of Chrysopogon fulvus is present near the watchtower; this is a preferred grazing area for gaur. During the June 2024 check, no fresh tiger signs were recorded, but pugmarks from the previous month were noted at km 13.4. The area is considered a potential corridor for tigers moving between the eastern and western blocks.

documents.title: Nilgiri Wildlife Trust Administrative Correspondence
documents.content:
A list of the new floor plan is attached. The field staff will have a larger room on the ground floor, which should make it easier to store gear and also to hold briefings without disturbing the office work. I request all section heads to go through the plan and let me know if there are any major concerns by the 10th of January. Minor adjustments can be made on site after the move.

I will be sending out a separate circular regarding the telephone and internet setup. For now, please note that our phone numbers will change. The new numbers will be shared once the BSNL line is active. Our email addresses remain the same.

Thank you for your cooperation. Let's make this move as smooth as possible.

Regards,
R. Krishnan
Admin Officer

---

**From:** M. Velayudham, Field Director
**To:** R. Krishnan, Admin Officer
**Cc:** S. Menon, Accounts; T. Bala, Procurement
**Subject:** RE: Office Relocation – Final Schedule and Packing Instructions
**Date:** 06 January 2024

Krishnan ji,

Received your mail. The schedule is fine. But one request – the field equipment store has some items that are sensitive to dust and moisture. The camera traps, the GPS units, and the spare batteries especially. When the packers handle these, I want one of our own staff to be present and supervise. I will depute Suresh from my team to be there on the 20th and 21st. He knows which boxes are fragile. Please instruct the packers to listen to him. Also, we have about twenty old field boots and some raincoats in the store that are beyond repair. I suggest we dispose of them rather than move them. I will make a list and send it to you for approval. It is no use paying to transport rubbish to the new office.

One more thing. The new office plan shows the field room on the ground floor. That is good. But we also need a small lockable cupboard in that room for the keys to the vehicle and the store. There is no cupboard shown in the plan. Can you add one? We had a small issue last month where the key was misplaced and we had to break the lock. We do not want a repeat.

Regards,
M. Velayudham

---

The Trust's administrative records list its headquarters_city as Coimbatore. Record status: current.

Velayudham ji,

Noted. I will instruct the packers about the sensitive equipment. And yes, we will add a lockable cupboard to the field room plan. I will mark it on the layout and send you the revised copy by Monday.

Regarding the old boots and raincoats, please send the list. I will get it approved and we can discard them before the move. No point in shifting unusable items.

DOCUMENT S03-01: SURVEY AREA DEFINITION AND ROUTE PROTOCOL
Version 2.1 | Revision Date: 05 January 2024
Prepared by: Survey Planning Cell, Northern Wildlife Trust (NWT)
Distribution: Field Coordinators, Team Leaders, Data Entry Cell

1. PURPOSE
This document defines the survey areas, routes, and field protocols for the 2024 NWT survey programme in the Mudumalai–Sigur landscape. It supersedes Version 2.0 (dated 18 November 2023). All field teams must carry a printed copy of the relevant route sheets and the area maps referenced in Section 5.

2. SURVEY AREA REGISTER
The following survey blocks are active for the 2024 season. Area figures are derived from the 2023 ground-truthing exercise and the 2024 boundary re-survey; they are current as of 01 January 2024.

| Block Code | Block Name | Survey Area (ha) | Status | Remarks |
|------------|----------------------|------------------|-------------|-----------------------------------------|
| MTR-A1 | Mudumalai Core North | 320 | Current | Main tiger habitat block; see Note 2.1 |
| MTR-A2 | Mudumalai Core South | 285 | Current | Includes Moyar gorge riparian strip |
| MTR-B1 | Sigur Plateau West | 410 | Current | Elephant corridor zone; dry deciduous |
| MTR-B2 | Sigur Plateau East | 265 | Current | Scrub–grassland mosaic; low water access |
| MTR-C1 | Buffer North | 150 | Current | Agricultural interface; high human use |
| MTR-C2 | Buffer South | 120 | Current | Proposed extension under review |
| MTR-D1 | Moyar Gorge | 95 | Current | Steep terrain; limited patrol access |

Note 2.1: The NWT survey plan 2024 specifies that the Mudumalai Tiger Reserve survey_area_hectares is 320 hectares. Record status: current. This figure corresponds to Block MTR-A1 and is the current controlled entry for the reserve's primary survey block. No revision is pending for this entry as of the 05 January 2024 update.

3. ROUTE DESCRIPTIONS

3.1 Route MTR-A1/R1 (Mudumalai Core North – Ridge Line)
- Start: Junction of Forest Road 7 and the old elephant wall (GPS: 11.573°N, 76.632°E)
- End: Moyar viewpoint cairn (GPS: 11.589°N, 76.618°E)
- Length: 6.2 km
- Terrain: Gentle ridge gradient; open dry deciduous forest; moderate ground cover.
- Habitat notes: Predominant species – Terminalia alata, Anogeissus latifolia, and Grewia tiliifolia. Dense understorey in drainage lines. Bamboo clumps observed at km 3.1 and km 4.8.
- Patrol time (walking): 3.5–4.0 hours.
- Water sources: Seasonal stream at km 2.4 (dry by late February in normal years); check at km 5.0 for rock pools.

3.2 Route MTR-A1/R2 (Mudumalai Core North – Valley Loop)
- Start: Forest Rest House, Masinagudi side gate
- End: Same point (loop)
- Length: 8.7 km
- Terrain: Mixed valley floor and lower slope; includes one major stream crossing (knee-deep during monsoon, impassable at peak flow).
- Habitat notes: Riparian vegetation along the stream; large Ficus trees at km 3.2 and km 6.5. Evidence of gaur and sambar congregation at km 4.0–4.5.
- Patrol time (walking): 5.0–5.5 hours.
- Special instruction: During monsoon (June–September), use the alternate high-ground track at km 2.8 if stream level exceeds mid-calf.

3.3 Route MTR-A2/R1 (Mudumalai Core South – Gorge Edge)
- Start: Moyar bridge, south bank
- End: Old watchtower ruins
- Length: 4.9 km
- Terrain: Steep sections; loose rock at km 1.5–2.0; narrow path along gorge rim.
- Habitat notes: Dry thorn scrub with Carissa spinarum and Ziziphus mauritiana. Good visibility into gorge; vulture nesting sites on opposite cliff face.
- Patrol time (walking): 4.0–4.5 hours.
- Water sources: None reliable; carry minimum 2 L per person.

- Patrol time (walking): 3.5–4.0 hours.
- Water sources: None reliable; carry minimum 2 L per person.

4. PATROL ROUTE 14 (ENT23) — DETAILED DESCRIPTION

4.1 Route Identification and Status

Patrol Route 14 (Route Code: PR-14; also referred to as Route 14 or R14 in patrol logs and field communications) is a designated patrol route under the Northern Block survey programme. 4.2 Route Start and End Points

- End: Moyar viewpoint cairn (GPS: 11.589°N, 76.618°E) — shared endpoint with Route MTR-A1/R1

4.3 Terrain and Path Description

The route follows a mostly gentle gradient along the northern ridge, with two moderate ascents at km 3.2–3.8 and km 9.0–9.4. The path is wide enough for two people to walk abreast for most of the length; narrow sections occur at km 5.5–5.8 where the path passes between rock outcrops. Surface is packed earth with loose gravel patches, particularly after the dry-season fire lines. At km 11.2, the path crosses a dry nullah; the crossing is straightforward except during peak monsoon flow, when the water level can reach mid-calf.

documents.content:
---

5. PATROL ROUTE 17 (ENT24) — DETAILED DESCRIPTION

5.1 Route Identification and Status

Patrol Route 17 (Route Code: PR-17; also referred to as Route 17 or R17 in
patrol logs and field communications) is a designated patrol route under
the Northern Block survey programme, running along the eastern edge of the
reserve. The patrol map indicates that Patrol Route 17 patrol_route_length_km
is 18.2 kilometers. Record status: current. This figure is the current
controlled entry for the route; it was verified against GPS track logs
during the February 2024 field check and no revision is pending as of the
15 March 2024 update. Older map sheets showing a length of 17.5 km or 19 km
should be disregarded; the 18.2 km figure supersedes all earlier
approximations.

5.2 Route Start and End Points

- Start: Forest check-post at Kambanur gate (GPS: 11.622°N, 76.634°E)
- End: Old teak plantation boundary cairn (GPS: 11.607°N, 76.660°E) —
  shared endpoint with Route MTR-B2/R4

The patrol map indicates that Patrol Route 17 patrol_route_length_km is 18.2 kilometers. Record status: current.

5.3 Terrain and Path Description

The route begins on a wide motorable track for the first 2.1 km, passing
the Kambanur waterhole. At km 2.1 the path narrows to a single-file trail
climbing steadily through mixed dry deciduous forest. The gradient is
moderate but sustained until km 4.6, where the trail levels out along a
ridge line with open views to the east. From km 4.6 to km 9.3 the path
follows the ridge crest with gentle undulations; the surface is laterite
with scattered loose stones, requiring care during the wet season. At
km 9.3 the trail descends into a shallow valley, crossing a seasonal
stream at km 10.1. The crossing is dry from January to May but can be
knee-deep during monsoon flows. From km 10.1 to km 14.0 the path runs
through fairly open woodland with good visibility; the surface is packed
earth with a few eroded sections at km 12.4–12.7 and km 13.2–13.5. The
final 4.2 km section, from km 14.0 to the end, climbs moderately through
denser forest, with the last 600 m along the boundary of the old teak
plantation. The path is generally well defined throughout; no major
obstructions were recorded during the February 2024 field check.

5.4 Habitat Notes

The eastern block of the route is dominated by dry thorn scrub up to km
4.6, with Acacia planifrons and Prosopis juliflora common. The ridge
section (km 4.6–9.3) carries mixed dry deciduous forest; the canopy is
open and the ground layer is grassy, supporting a good population of
chital and occasionally sambar. The valley section (km 9.3–14.0) has
denser undergrowth with Lantana camara thickets, particularly along the
stream course. Fresh tiger pugmarks were recorded at km 11.6 in early
February 2024, and a scat sample was collected for analysis. The final
section (km 14.0–18.2) is predominantly older secondary forest with
larger trees, including Terminalia bellirica and Pterocarpus marsupium.
Sloth bear diggings are common in this section, and the old teak
plantation boundary is a known corridor for elephant movement between the
northern and eastern blocks.

5.5 Patrol Time and Recommended Schedule

- Patrol time (walking): 7.5–9.0 hours, depending on stops, terrain
  conditions, and the monsoon status of the stream crossing.
- Recommended start time: 05:30 hours during the dry season (to complete
  the route before peak heat); 06:00 hours during the monsoon.
- Recommended frequency: Twice per week during the dry season; once per
  week during the monsoon, weather permitting. The stream crossing at
  km 10.1 should be checked before departure during the monsoon; if the
  water level is above mid-calf, the route should be postponed by a day.

During the monsoon (June–September), the usual start point at the eastern gate may be inaccessible due to waterlogging. An alternate start point has been identified at the junction of the old fire line and the cart track, approximately 1.2 km north of the eastern gate.

- **Start Point ER-2A:** Latitude 11°34'20"N, Longitude 76°58'45"E
- **Access:** From the Range Office, take the main road towards the eastern gate; turn left at the fire line marker (painted yellow) and follow the fire line for 1.2 km. The track is usable by gypsy during dry weather; during heavy rain, walk from the fire line marker (approx. 20 minutes).
- **Route Joining:** From ER-2A, walk south-west along the fire line for 0.8 km to join the main route at km 1.4. The joining section is open with moderate grass; visibility is good.
- **Patrol Time Impact:** The alternate start adds approximately 0.5 hours to the total patrol time (walking from fire line marker or driving to ER-2A). Recommended start time during monsoon: 05:45 hours.
- **Status:** This alternate start point was field-checked on 12 June 2024 and is currently operational. The fire line is clear of obstructions; the cart track has two minor ruts at km 0.3 and km 0.7, passable by gypsy.

---

**5.8 Habitat Notes – Alternate Start Section**

The alternate start section (ER-2A to km 1.4) passes through dry thorn scrub with scattered Cassia fistula and Ziziphus mauritiana. The ground layer is sparse, with frequent bare patches. Porcupine diggings are common. A small seasonal stream crosses the fire line at approximately 0.4 km from ER-2A; this stream is dry from January to May but may flow after heavy rain. No major wildlife signs were recorded during the June 2024 check, other than a few old elephant droppings near the stream crossing.

---

**5.9 Route ER-3 – Northern Ridge Survey Route**

**Route Code:** ER-3
**Block:** Northern Ridge
**Total Length:** 15.6 km
**Survey Area:** 420 hectares (including 60 hectares of the old teak plantation boundary)
**Last Revised:** March 2024

documents.content:
**5.10 Route ER-4 – Western Slopes Reconnaissance Route**

**Route Code:** ER-4  
**Block:** Western Slopes  
**Total Length:** 18.2 km  
**Survey Area:** 510 hectares (including 45 hectares of riparian fringe along the Vanam River)  
**Last Revised:** June 2024  
**Revision History:** v1.0 (Feb 2023), v2.0 (Nov 2023), v3.0 (Jun 2024 – current)

**Purpose:** This route covers the western boundary of the survey block, including the riparian corridor and the transition zone between dry deciduous forest and moist deciduous forest. The route is primarily used for dry-season wildlife census and vegetation transects. It is not recommended for monsoon patrols beyond km 6.0 due to stream crossings.

**Route Description:**

- **Start Point ER-4A:** Latitude 11°31'08"N, Longitude 76°55'12"E. Located at the western gate near the check dam. Parking available for one gypsy; the gate is locked during non-working hours. Key with the Range Office.
- **km 0.0–2.5:** Flat terrain along the Vanam River bank. Dense riparian vegetation with Terminalia arjuna and Syzygium cumini. The river is perennial; water level is high during monsoon (June–September). Elephant crossing point observed at km 1.1; fresh dung and footprints recorded on most patrols.
- **km 2.5–6.0:** Gradual ascent towards the ridge. Mixed dry deciduous forest with Anogeissus latifolia and Hardwickia binata. The old fire line runs parallel to the route on the eastern side; it was cleared in May 2024 and is currently usable. At km 4.3, a seasonal stream crosses the route; this stream is dry from January to May but may flow after heavy rain. A small bridge (single log) is present; condition is poor and should be checked before use.
- **km 6.0–10.8:** Steep ascent to the ridge top. Rocky outcrops with sparse vegetation. Sloth bear signs (diggings and claw marks on trees) are common in this section. A water hole at km 7.9 (approx. 8 m diameter, depth 0.5 m during dry season) is a reliable water source for wildlife; camera trap placement recommended here.
- **km 10.8–15.2:** Ridge top with open grassland patches. Views over the western valley. Gaur herds are frequently sighted in the morning. A watchtower (wooden, 4 m high) is located at km 12.6; it was repaired in April 2024 and is in good condition. The tower is suitable for two persons.
- **km 15.2–18.2:** Descent towards the northern boundary. Moderate slope with dense undergrowth. The route joins the Northern Ridge route (ER-3) at km 15.6 of ER-3. The joining point is marked with a yellow-painted stone.

**Patrol Time Estimate:** 6.5 to 7.5 hours (walking, with 30-minute rest at the watchtower). Driving is possible up to km 2.5 during dry weather; beyond that, the route is walk-only.

**Habitat Notes – Riparian Section (km 0.0–2.5):**

The riparian fringe is narrow (10–25 m on each bank) but supports high biodiversity. During the June 2024 check, the following were recorded: otter tracks at km 0.8, a pair of crested serpent eagles nesting at km 1.6, and several large Terminalia arjuna trees with active hornbill nests. The understory is dominated by Lantana camara in patches, particularly near the check dam. This invasive species has spread approximately 200 m downstream since the January 2024 survey. Control measures (manual uprooting) are planned for the dry season of 2025.

**Habitat Notes – Ridge Top Section (km 10.8–15.2):**

The grassland patches are maintained by occasional fire; the last fire was in February 2024. Grass height ranges from 0.3 m to 1.2 m. A small patch of Chrysopogon fulvus is present near the watchtower; this is a preferred grazing area for gaur. During the June 2024 check, no fresh tiger signs were recorded, but pugmarks from the previous month were noted at km 13.4. The area is considered a potential corridor for tigers moving between the eastern and western blocks.
